rounds.text: Propshop Events and Exhibitions Ltd trades at an exceptionally modest P/E ratio of 12.4x [E1], despite underlying fundamental metrics that vastly outperform its sector benchmarks. The company delivers an outstanding return on equity of 41.46% against a sector benchmark of just 5.35% [E6], alongside an ROCE of 57.03% that completely dwarfs the sector median of 6.91% [E7]. This phenomenal profitability is backed by strong multi-year compounding, with 3-year sales growth at 40% [E10] and 3-year profit growth reaching an incredible 102% [E12]. Furthermore, the business is practically debt-free with a debt-to-equity ratio of only 0.01x [E21], while operating margins have successfully expanded by 6 percentage points to 16% over the last three years [E17]. The discounted cash flow model indicates a substantial margin of safety of 69.6% [E28], with a reverse DCF implying that the current market price accounts for a mere 1.6% earnings growth [E29]. Conceded: cash conversion is weak at 0.02x for Mar 2025 [E20], and debtor days have increased from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E35].

The most significant risk to the valuation is a near-total failure to convert reported profits into actual cash, evidenced by a cash conversion ratio of just 0.02x for March 2025 [E20]. This disconnect between earnings and liquidity is exacerbated by deteriorating operational efficiency, as debtor days have climbed from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E35]. Despite these liquidity concerns, the market is pricing the company at a P/B of 2.44x, which represents a significant premium over the sector benchmark of 1.38x [E5]. Investors should also be wary of the underlying business stability, given that both yearly and quarterly operating-margin trends are currently inconsistent [E18][E19]. Conceded: the company has demonstrated strong historical compounded profit growth of 102% over three years [E12] and maintains a high return on equity of 52.3% [E9]. Conceded: the P/E ratio remains at 12.4x [E1] and the firm is almost debt-free with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.01x [E21][E33]. However, the lack of any dividend yield [E3] and a low-confidence neutral rating from rules-based screens [E36] suggest that high growth figures may not yet translate into tangible shareholder value.

Conceded: the cash conversion ratio for March 2025 is low at 0.02x [E20] and debtor days have increased from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E35]. Conceded: the price-to-book ratio of 2.44x sits above the sector benchmark of 1.38x [E5], yearly and quarterly operating-margin trends are inconsistent [E18][E19], and there is no dividend yield [E3]. However, the bear understates the sheer magnitude of the fundamental outperformance that justifies this premium, specifically an elite ROE of 52.3% and ROCE of 70.7% that completely dwarfs the sector benchmarks of 5.35% and 6.91% respectively [E5][E6][E7][E9]. Furthermore, the company's financial position is exceptionally secure with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.01x and recognized positive status as almost debt-free [E21][E33]. The discount in valuation is laid bare by a reverse DCF showing today's price implies a meager 1.6% earnings growth against an 18.0% base case [E29], completely belying historical compounded profit growth of 102% over 3 years [E12]. Finally, the bear's dismissal ignores a substantial discounted cash flow intrinsic value providing a 69.6% margin of safety [E27][E28].

Conceded: the company maintains high ROE and ROCE [E8][E9] and remains almost debt-free [E33] with a low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.01x [E21]. However, the Bull’s reliance on these returns ignores a clear downward trend, as median ROE has dropped from 67% over five years [E14] and 64% over three years [E15] to 52% last year [E16]. The Bull’s growth projections and DCF margin of safety [E27][E28][E29] are fundamentally compromised by a cash conversion ratio of only 0.02x, which proves that reported profits are not translating into actual cash flow [E20]. This liquidity risk is underscored by debtor days rising from 40.2 to 56.8 [E35], while borrowings have actually increased from zero to Rs 0.17 Cr in the latest period [E22]. Furthermore, the Bull’s growth narrative is undermined by a sharp deceleration in compounded profit growth, falling from a three-year rate of 102% [E12] to just 27% over the trailing twelve months [E13]. Finally, the inconsistency in both yearly and quarterly operating margins [E18][E19] suggests the business lacks the stability required to support the Bull's aggressive DCF assumptions [E27][E29].
